A quivering is a small, rapid, repeated trembling or shaking movement — one that happens very quickly and usually without much force. It is not a big, violent shake. It is a slight, fast, continuous flutter, almost as if something is vibrating in place.

Think of a plucked guitar string right after you release it — it doesn't swing wildly side to side, it vibrates very quickly in a tiny space. That delicate, rapid motion is a quivering.

A quivering is usually caused by one of three things:

1. Strong emotions felt inside the body
When a person feels intense fear, cold, excitement, grief, or nervousness, their body can produce tiny, uncontrollable tremors. These are quiverings. The body is overwhelmed, and that overflow shows up physically.

The quivering of her hands gave away how frightened she really was.

2. Physical weakness or effort
Muscles that are exhausted, in pain, or struggling under strain can begin to quiver. Athletes feel this after intense exercise. Someone holding a heavy weight for too long will notice a quivering in their arms.

After the long climb, there was a constant quivering in his legs.

3. Natural forces or vibrations acting on a light object
Thin, lightweight things — leaves, flames, water surfaces, voice — can be set into quivering by wind, sound waves, or any slight disturbance.

The quivering of the candle flame told us a window somewhere was open.
The Quality of the Motion — What Makes It "Quivering" Specifically

This is where precision matters.

A quivering is not just any shaking. It has a specific character:

  • Small in size — the movement covers very little space. It is not thrashing or swinging.
  • Fast in speed — the back-and-forth happens very rapidly.
  • Continuous — it doesn't happen once and stop; it keeps repeating in a quick rhythm.
  • Often involuntary — the person or object experiencing it usually cannot control it.

This combination — small + fast + continuous + uncontrolled — is what makes a quivering different from a shake (which is bigger and more forceful) or a tremble (which is very similar, but "trembling" often implies more sustained, visible movement, while "quivering" suggests something finer and more delicate).
Where Quivering Commonly Appears (as a noun)

The word pairs naturally with certain parts of the body and certain situations:

  • Lips — "the quivering of her lips before she cried"
  • Chin — a classic sign of suppressed tears
  • Hands or fingers — nervousness, cold, fear, or old age
  • Voice — when emotion makes someone's voice shake slightly as they speak
  • Eyelids or nostrils — in moments of strong feeling
  • Leaves, flames, or water — in natural descriptions
The Emotional Weight of the Word

"Quivering" carries a sense of vulnerability. When you describe a quivering, you are almost always pointing to something or someone that is on the edge — overwhelmed by emotion, pushed to physical limits, or moved by an external force they cannot resist.

This is why the word appears often in emotional, dramatic, or tender writing. It reveals something that the person might be trying to hide but cannot. A quivering is honest. The body tells the truth even when the person does not.

Despite his calm voice, the quivering of his jaw told everyone in the room that he was barely holding himself together.

A quivering (noun) is:

A small, rapid, continuous, involuntary trembling movement — in a body part, a voice, or a physical object — usually caused by strong emotion, physical strain, or a light external force.

It signals intensity beneath the surface — something that is too much to be contained completely, leaking out through tiny, fast, repeated motion.
